author: NewsBreak
title: Newsom Blasts Trump Administration Over Hydrogen Hub Funding Cut in California - NewsBreak
text:
1 hours ago SACRAMENTO — Governor Gavin Newsom sharply criticized the Trump administration after the U.S. Department of Energy canceled a $1.2 billion funding commitment for California’s Alliance for Renewable Clean Hydrogen Energy Systems (ARCHES). The decision threatens a project that state leaders say is key to California’s clean energy future.
Photo by Possessed Photography on Unsplash “In Trump’s America, energy policy is set by the highest bidder, economics and common sense be damned,” Newsom said in a statement. “Clean hydrogen deserves to be part of California’s energy future — creating hundreds of thousands of new jobs and saving billions in health costs. We’ll continue to pursue an all-of-the above clean energy strategy that powers our future and cleans the air, no matter what DC tries to dictate.”
The cancellation jeopardizes more than $10 billion in private sector investment and puts at risk 200,000 projected jobs, according to the state. It also undermines anticipated annual savings of nearly $3 billion in health costs.
U.S. Senator Alex Padilla echoed Newsom’s criticism. “The cancellation of ARCHES is vindictive, shortsighted, and proof this Administration is not serious about American energy dominance,” Padilla said. “Walking away from ARCHES threatens the future promise of hydrogen energy and will guarantee energy costs continue to rise for families while the rest of the world surges ahead in its development. California will not back down—we’ll keep leading on clean energy where this Administration has chosen to abandon American leadership.”
ARCHES, based in California and backed by over 400 partners, was designed to accelerate renewable hydrogen adoption across industries. In 2023, the Department of Energy selected the project to negotiate funding, and by July 2024 ARCHES became the first hub to sign a cooperative agreement, the largest in the agency’s history.
Despite the federal setback, California officials say the state will continue advancing renewable hydrogen, building on its broader climate progress. Greenhouse gas emissions are down 20 percent since 2000 while the economy grew 78 percent, making California the world’s fourth largest economy. In 2023, the state was powered by two-thirds clean energy, with daily periods reaching 100 percent clean electricity.
State leaders emphasize that ARCHES remains central to California’s plan to meet its goal of carbon neutrality by 2045.
